cover.artAlt: A Tyrannosaurus rex standing in a misty prehistoric forest at sunrise
cover.blurb: They ruled the Earth for over 160 million years. Turn the page and go back in time.

pages.title: Three Horns and a Giant Shield
pages.artAlt: A herd of Triceratops grazing on ferns in an open prehistoric plain

facts.text: Triceratops means three-horned face. Two long horns grew above its eyes and a shorter one sat on its nose, above a wide bony frill that spread out behind its head.
facts.source: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History (naturalhistory.si.edu)

facts.text: Its skull was one of the biggest heads any land animal has ever had, longer than a grown-up is tall.
facts.artAlt: A mounted Triceratops skull in a museum hall, its two long brow horns and wide bony frill lit from above, with a person standing beside it for size
facts.caption: One skull, longer than the person standing beside it.

facts.text: Triceratops ate only plants. It had hundreds of teeth stacked in tight bundles that worked like scissors, slicing through tough ferns and branches.
facts.artAlt: A close view of the jaw of a Triceratops skull, showing small teeth packed tightly together in long rows along the bone
facts.caption: Teeth packed in tight bundles, built for slicing tough plants.

infographic.title: How big was a Triceratops?

rows.label: A kid your age, head to toe

infographic.caption: The 30 feet comes from the Natural History Museum in London. The kid and the car are everyday sizes, here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: The Long-Necked Giants
pages.artAlt: Long-necked Brachiosaurus wading in a calm lake at sunset, reaching into tall trees

facts.text: Brachiosaurus had front legs that were longer than its back legs, so its whole body sloped upward and its head was carried very high, like a living crane.
The long-necked dinosaurs did not chew. They raked leaves off branches with peg-shaped teeth and swallowed them whole, letting their enormous stomachs do the rest of the work.
facts.artAlt: A close view of a long-necked dinosaur skull in a museum case, its long peg-shaped teeth leaning out from the front of the jaw like the tines of a rake
facts.caption: Peg-shaped teeth, made for raking leaves off a branch.

facts.text: These giants, called sauropods, were the largest animals that ever walked on land. The biggest one we have found weighed as much as ten elephants put together.
facts.artAlt: An enormous long-necked dinosaur skeleton fills a museum hall, its neck stretching up and out over the heads of the tiny visitors below
facts.caption: A long-necked giant in a museum hall, with people small beneath it.

infographic.title: How heavy was the biggest long-neck?
infographic.caption: The 70 tons, and the elephant it is measured in, both come from the American Museum of Natural History, which weighs this dinosaur at ten African elephants. The family car is an everyday weight, here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: Some Dinosaurs Had Feathers
pages.artAlt: A feathered Velociraptor standing alert in tall grass

facts.text: The real Velociraptor was about the size of a turkey, not the tall movie monster. Most of its length was a long, stiff tail it used for balance.
Fossil arm bones from Velociraptor have small bumps on them called quill knobs. On birds today, those same bumps are where feathers attach, so we know this dinosaur had feathers.
facts.artAlt: A fossil Velociraptor arm bone lying on dark cloth, a neat row of small round bumps standing up along one edge of the bone
facts.caption: Then: quill knobs on a fossil arm, where feathers once attached.

facts.text: Birds are dinosaurs. Every sparrow and pigeon you see is descended from small feathered dinosaurs, which means one branch of the dinosaur family never went extinct.
facts.artAlt: A house sparrow perched on a garden fence in bright daylight, feathers puffed out and one scaly clawed foot gripping the wood
facts.caption: Now: the same feathers and the same scaly feet, on your fence.

pages.title: How We Know Any of This
pages.artAlt: A dinosaur skeleton half-uncovered at a fossil dig site in orange desert rock

facts.text: A fossil is not the original bone. When a dinosaur was buried quickly by mud or sand, minerals seeped in over millions of years and slowly turned the bone to stone.
Fossil hunters dig with brushes, dental picks and small hand tools, because a hammer would smash the very thing they came to find. Big bones get wrapped in a plaster jacket for the trip home.
facts.artAlt: A hand holds a small soft brush and sweeps orange dust off a half-buried fossil bone, with a pointed dental pick resting on the rock beside it
facts.caption: A brush and a dental pick, doing the slow careful work.

facts.text: Dinosaurs lived for over 160 million years. The last of them, apart from birds, died out about 66 million years ago after an enormous asteroid struck the Earth.
facts.artAlt: A close view of a desert cliff face showing stacked bands of orange and cream rock, with one thin pale line running straight across the middle of them
facts.caption: One thin line in the rock is the day everything changed.

infographic.title: How long ago was all of this?

stops.label: The very first dinosaurs walk the Earth
An asteroid strikes, and the last of the big dinosaurs die out
Mud and sand press down on the buried bones and turn them to stone
Fossil hunters brush that stone free, and the birds outside are still dinosaurs

infographic.caption: Both dates come from the Natural History Museum in London, which puts the first dinosaurs at about 230 million years ago and the end of the big ones at 66 million years ago.
